lines.text: Thousands of islands strung across the equator, home to ancient empires, spice traders and fiery volcanoes. This is the story of Indonesia.
About a million years ago early humans, Homo erectus, were already living on Java. Their fossils were found there in 1891.
Some seventy thousand years ago Toba in Sumatra erupted, one of the largest blasts in two million years, leaving a vast lake behind.
From the seventh century, the Buddhist sea empire of Srivijaya ruled the Strait of Malacca, rich on the trade between India and China.
In central Java, builders raised Borobudur, a vast stepped Buddhist monument covered in hundreds of carved scenes.
Nearby rose Prambanan, its tall Hindu towers dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma.
In 1257 the Samalas volcano on Lombok exploded so violently that it cooled the world, though for centuries no one knew where it was.
In 1293 the Majapahit empire arose on Java, and under Gajah Mada and Hayam Wuruk it held sway over much of the islands.
In 1527 the port that would become Jakarta was founded, later the Dutch town of Batavia.
As Islam spread along the trade routes, the Muslim sultanate of Mataram came to rule much of Java.
In 1602 the Dutch East India Company was founded. With forts, fleets and armies it seized the spice trade.
When the company collapsed, the Dutch state took over, and the Dutch East Indies sent spices, sugar, coffee and rubber to Europe.
In 1883 Krakatoa blew apart. Its tsunamis killed tens of thousands, and its ash dimmed sunsets around the world.
In 1901 Sukarno was born, the man who would lead the independence movement and become the first president.
Suharto, born twenty years later, would be the general who took power from him.
And Pramoedya Ananta Toer would become the nation's great novelist, writing much of his Buru Quartet as a political prisoner.
In 1945 Indonesia was born, a nation of hundreds of peoples, and today the largest Muslim population on Earth.
But the Dutch came back, and four years of war and diplomacy followed before independence was recognised in 1949.
It had all begun on the seventeenth of August 1945, when Sukarno read the proclamation, two days after Japan surrendered.
In 1951 Prabowo Subianto was born, a future general who would become president in 2024.
In 1955 Sukarno hosted leaders of newly free nations from Asia and Africa at Bandung, speaking out against colonialism.
Meanwhile Bali, with its Hindu temples, rice terraces and dance, was becoming one of the world's best-loved islands.
In 1961 Joko Widodo was born, a furniture seller who would rise from mayor to president.
In 1965, after a failed coup, the army led the killing of hundreds of thousands of alleged communists, and Suharto rose to power.
In 1980 Komodo National Park was created to protect the Komodo dragon, the largest lizard on Earth.
In 1998 Suharto fell after more than thirty years, and the era of Reformasi brought democracy back.
East Timor, long occupied, voted to leave, and in 2002 became an independent nation.
That October bombs tore through Bali's nightclubs, killing two hundred and two people.
On Boxing Day 2004 an undersea quake off Sumatra sent a tsunami across the Indian Ocean, and Indonesia was struck hardest.
And now a new capital, Nusantara, is rising on Borneo, to take over from crowded and sinking Jakarta.
From Java Man to Nusantara, Indonesia keeps building its future across a sea of islands.
